p: DOE's Restorative Justice Program operates at approximately 972 schools at a cost of approximately $12 million annually. How much was allocated or set aside in the Preliminary Budget for restorative justice programs?
So the actual number of schools is 987, and their overall budget is $16.8 million.

(UNINTELLIGIBLE) Okay. And then how much was allocated in the-- so that's for this current fiscal year, $16.8 million. Thank you for the correction. And how much was allocated or proposed in the Preliminary Budget?

The budget is still under review and being finalized.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 155 Committee on Public Safety
Well, there was a Preliminary Budget that was...
(UN-MIC’D) (INAUDIBLE)
proposed.
That initial cost was $12 million.
Okay, $12 million, so that's a gap of $4.8 million in the restorative justice programs?
Correct.

Okay. And what are your-- I’m under the assumption, given your testimony, that the restorative justice programs are successful. We like them, we're fans, everyone on the Council likes them, and we're fans of them. Why was it proposed to cut funding to restorative justice programs if it's generally agreed upon that these are successful programs and generally successful in reducing suspensions and things that detract from our schoolwork?

I don't know that restorative is cut as the budget is not finalized, as you know. I will...

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 156 Committee on Public Safety
It was a proposed cut, so you know it's not finalized...
proposed (INAUDIBLE)
but it was proposed to be cut.
Right. But I don't know if that's final. So I don't want to go on record to say that that's final as it relates to restorative.
Okay, obviously budgets are ongoing...
That’s correct.

But just know that this Council is committed to restorative justice practices. Now, in the DOE details in The Terms and Conditions Report, I know you said 987, but the terms and conditions say 972. I'm interested in the discrepancy there, but there are restorative justice programs, and schools fall into direct and indirect categories. And can you discuss the differences between these designations, especially as they relate to staffing and programming?

We're going to have one of our restorative team members who is deeply

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 157 Committee on Public Safety engrossed in the work, as well as the financing and programming, to talk to you more about those designations of direct and indirect.
Okay, please raise your right hand.
Hi, Emilie Mittiga.
Hi. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your answers before these committees?
I do
Thank you. Please state your name again for the record, Emily Mittiga.
Thank you.

The discrepancy between the 972 and the 987, the 972 is last year's number. And when we saw some of our schools closed and/or collapsed, like middle, you know, a middle school may have been consolidated with a high school into one new (INAUDIBLE). And so that's how we have the difference in the two numbers. And we have the...

Sorry, what is the number of-- if two different schools had restorative justice, and they combined to one school, wouldn't

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 158 Committee on Public Safety that have decreased the number of schools that had restorative justice programs?
Yeah. So each year, we see some schools close, other schools open, and some schools consolidate. And then... (CROSS-TALK)
You're saying more schools open than closed, more schools added restorative justice programs, right?
Yeah. So we...
Okay.

And then there are some years that an individual school gets added to the program because of a specific need. A Superintendent makes a request to add that school because there's an extraordinary circumstance going on at the school, and they weren't previously on the list.
Okay.
So those are the things that account for the change in number between years.
Thank you. And can you differentiate between direct and indirect categories?

Yes. So, given our current central staffing capacity, we have the two

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 159 Committee on Public Safety different categories: direct schools receive a coach. They receive access to our full menu of trainings. They receive access to our centralized youth programming. They receive access to our entire curriculum. Whereas the indirect schools, although they have someone from our central team assigned to them, don't get constant implementation coaching. They don't necessarily have access to all the things that I just described. So they do have access to our full training catalog and our curricula, but they don't have somebody going in and coaching them on a regular basis around the implementation.
And, then...
Sorry, the direct schools also have access to funding to be able to fund teams at the school to do the work.

Great. And have you assessed, similar to the Project PIVOT question about assessment, have you evaluated the efficacy of direct coaching-- direct services versus indirect service-- direct services versus indirect services as it relates to things like suspension rates, things like academic outcomes, things like student satisfaction, teacher satisfaction?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 160 Committee on Public Safety

Yes. And so the direct services really speak to the investment of the school community in the restorative practices. And obviously, the more people and the more dedicated you are to these practices, you're going to see those greater outcomes. So we do see a difference in direct schools versus the indirect schools. We would love for all of our schools to be direct schools. That means more people are providing those respective services. And just like the NYPD giving you real-time correction and real-time data, I don't want to walk out of here and have you say bad things about me.
I would never. I would say bad things about your data, but not about you.
(LAUGHS) The Preliminary Budget was actually $10.8 million. The overall was $16.8 million with a $6 million gap.

So there's a $6 million gap that's different than the $4 million gap. Okay, thank you. I appreciate the correction, the honesty, and the corrections.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 161 Committee on Public Safety So the direct services have a Restorative Justice Coordinator, and the indirect, uh, would not have a full-time restorative justice...
Dedicated person.
Dedicated person. And so, how many schools have a Restorative Justice Coordinator?

So let's be clear on the Restorative Justice Coordinator. The Restorative Justice Coordinator sounds like it's a person who is funded by Restorative to provide these restorative services. In the direct schools, they get funding to identify a staff member who is operating under that respective capacity, received (INAUDIBLE) before and after to provide Restorative training and supports to schools...
I just... Not forced overtime just for the session. Okay.

(LAUGHS) That’s not forced overtime. It's voluntary, right? And it is for the purposes of creating more training and involvement for kids. It's a mindset shift, as you know, and that's the premise of that direct service.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 162 Committee on Public Safety And as you would expect with direct services, you would see better outcomes from the schools.
Okay. But you're not strictly measuring, or you haven't identified elements that you are measuring to evaluate the impact of restorative justice and direct and indirect restorative justice services?

Yeah, no, we are. So when we look at schools that are implementing with fidelity over a three-year period, those direct schools that are getting all the supports that we described, we see significant decreases in suspensions, incident levels; we see increases in the number of interventions that are used outside of traditional punitive measures. Can I share them?
The answer is yes, you can share. (LAUGHS)

So, for example, schools in that subgroup see an 18% drop in principal suspension as compared to the City seeing a 3.3% drop when you compare--the three-year comparison period we did was 2023 to 2025.

And these are just direct...

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 163 Committee on Public Safety
These are the schools that were in that direct-- were receiving those direct services over a three-year period.
And what about indirect... (CROSS-TALK)
We are looking at, like you know, if they're engaging for three years (INAUDIBLE)... (CROSS-TALK)
Yes. So, restorative justice versus non-restorative justice schools — 18% versus 3 point whatever, whatever, 3.1%?
For principal suspensions.
Okay. And then the indirect, is there data related to the indirect?
I don't have the indirect subgroup set out in front of me, so we can...
Does the DOE have that data?

Yes, we have that data.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 164 Committee on Public Safety
Okay, can we get that during the hearing?
Not during the hearing, but we'll get it back to you as soon as we humanly possibly can. All right? All of the people in the back (INAUDIBLE)... (CROSS-TALK)
For $40 billion, I feel like you can send a text to get the data.
We probably can. Somebody's working on that. I just want to commit to it before the hearing considering time. But I will...

Okay. And 18% reduction is alarming in a very positive way, and I think it does show the causal relationship between restorative justice practices and positive impacts on our students. Checking in with the NYPD, Section, what did I say? Section 115-140 (Transcriber Note: 14-150), that quarterly report, do you know where I can find it yet?

Thanks very much, Mr. Chairman.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 165 Committee on Public Safety So this report is published, I'm happy to direct your staff to it online. It will reflect through December 2025, the reporting period within the School Safety Division, 3,417 civilians and 84 uniform officers.
But the report itself is quarterly per school. That's the deployment, that's what the report requires.
So it'll be reported on a quarterly basis. Generally speaking, we don't release information about specific school deployments because of security issues about putting that information out publicly.
Did we change the law?
I'm sorry, Mr. Chairman?

I'm sorry, I mean, I just want to read it again. Where is it? Where is it? It's on my computer. I'm pretty sure I have the most updated Administrative Code up, and I understand you say you don't report it. But the Administrative Code says the NYPD is to report on that data. And again, we were asking a lot of questions about the deployment: How many School

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 166 Committee on Public Safety Safety Agents are actually in our schools? Time and time again, we're hearing there are not enough School Safety Agents. You are telling us, well, there are, and we assign enough. But the data will help reveal what that actually is. And per Administrative Code 14, sorry, 14-150. “The report shall also include, for each school operated by the department of education to which school safety agents are assigned, the number of school safety agents, averaged for the quarter, assigned to each of those schools.” So I can ask you why the NYPD is choosing not to comply with the Administrative Code?

Mr. Chairman, I would need-- I can't give you the answer, as I sit here on this panel, about exactly what is going into that report. But what I can tell you is that, as a general matter, there are those concerns about school safety that reflect information that's released publicly, that could be potentially sensitive. And I'm very happy to take this back and figure out exactly what's going on here.

I would love for you to figure out what's going on. Because this was

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 167 Committee on Public Safety passed 25 years ago, a quarter century ago, my predecessor’s predecessor’s predecessor was a co-sponsor of this bill, and it's the law. So, unless there's something about which I'm not aware, why the law isn't being followed, I would fully expect these quarterly reports to be published on the website and sent to the City Council. I'm going to turn it over to my co-chair, Chair Feliz.

Thank you so much, Chair Dinowitz. So I want to move on to school crossing guards. I just want to ask some final questions related to the School Safety Agents. What is the most amount of overtime you've seen a School Safety Agent work in a month? The most overtime.
On average, it’s 33 hours a month as our budget management-- as Seth Severino stated.

Okay, 33 hours per month. So basically, they work almost like an extra week.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 168 Committee on Public Safety What's the most overtime you've seen a worker or a School Safety Agent work for an entire month in overtime?
I'm sorry, but that amount varies. Obviously, everything is based on the allotted budget that we have for overtime. There are people who like to work overtime, some others don't.
Right. Yeah, but what's the most you've seen a worker work in overtime? I know it varies; there's a ballpark, a range, but what's like on the higher end of overtime hours?
You could easily have a School Safety Agent working, you know, an average of 60 hours of overtime a month.

Hmm. Okay. What would you say are the top budgetary or the top needs of the School Safety Agent Division? We've heard a lot today about equipment and headcount. What would you say the top three needs, based on your knowledge of everything going on with the division, are?

So, what we typically do is we work with OMB regarding our needs, and basically,

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 169 Committee on Public Safety that process is through the budgetary process. We currently have a substantial budget. And I think what you're bringing up is the hiring issue, and it is separate from a budget issue, where we do have vacancies that are funded.
Right, but top... (CROSS-TALK)
And we are working to put in orders for equipment replacement as needed for the x-ray machines as well.

Right. So what would be the top three that (INAUDIBLE). It could be budgetary needs, headcount-related, or legislative operation. What are the top three needs that could help make your lives easier and the lives of the School Safety Agents?
Again, that's something we work out with OMB on a regular basis.
Right. So what are the top needs that you've heard people raise? I'm sure headcount is one of them. And this question is for the

What are the top issues that people generally come to you with related to School Safety Agent operations?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 170 Committee on Public Safety

Well, we're getting a larger inquiry now for certain schools requesting scanning, unannounced scanning, and wanting to become full-time scanning schools. So I would probably say, you know, in terms of operational needs, more equipment for scanning.

Okay, more equipment. Also, earlier today, the DOE mentioned that many of the x-ray machines break down on a daily basis. How many machines again do we have? And approximately how many break down on a daily basis or break down very often on a daily basis?

Respectfully, just as a clarification of the number of machines was shared by the School Safety Division, and the statement of daily breakdowns was not-- that didn't come from me, DOE. I just want to make that clear for the record.
On a daily basis, I think I heard you, but that's okay; they break down very often. Whatever we could (INAUDIBLE) on a statement...
You heard that from the Police Department, so...

Right.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 171 Committee on Public Safety
But I could clarify that, and I could repeat that. I said we have a total of 208 scanning x-ray machines, 276 open gates, and a total of 817 hand wands.
Okay, and approximately how many machines break down on a database? Would you say 10% of the machines break down on a daily basis, 5%?
It's a small percentage that might have malfunctions that could be easily repaired on the spot by our trained technicians.

Okay. All right, so I'll pause there on the School Safety Agents. We've spent a lot of time talking about School Safety Agents. It's four o’clock, it's almost three hours. School crossing guards, it seems, as many of my colleagues mentioned earlier today, seem like we're having similar issues: People from our communities requesting school crossing guards due to traffic violence-related incidents in their community, and people making their voices heard, reaching out to the local precinct, reaching out to

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 172 Committee on Public Safety the local Community Board, and these requests generally go unaddressed. Speaking about requests, a school principal, from one of the schools in my district, earlier today, emailed me and many others, basically saying that there was a child who was struck last year. Also, there have been many near-miss incidents near that East Tremont very busy corner, and the requests generally go unaddressed. So talk to us about the headcount for school crossing guards. I think you mentioned that earlier today, but just want to make it-- just want to have it fresh. And also, how many vacant positions? What's the actual headcount and the budgeted headcount in vacant positions for the school crossing guards?

Thank you for that question. As of April 13th, our authorized headcount is 2,309. Our actual head count is 2,160. So that leaves us with a vacancy of 149. We have 45 that are not accounted for in that number that are actually out long-term sick. We also have a class of

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 173 Committee on Public Safety 100 expected to enter and be hired on May 11th, 2026. So you add that 100 and that 45, and we're close to our actual headcount. In 2018, our actual headcount was 2,500. So in 2018, we had 340 more school crossing guards than we do today.
What is the pay for school crossing guards? I think you mentioned $19.00 an hour. Is there like different levels of pay depending on experience?

School crossing guards, Level I, are part-time employees. They make $19.14 per hour. They work five-hour tours, 2.5 hours in the morning from 7:00 to 9:30 a.m., and then 2.5 hours in the evening from 12:30 to 3:00. Our Level II guards are full-time employees who receive benefits. They get paid $44,533.

And in addition to what the Chief is saying, there's also a uniform allowance, as per their contract, for an additional $226.00. And there is a longevity differential, which is $0.43 of incremental cost for 15 years or more for Level I and $800.00 for Level II.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 174 Committee on Public Safety
How many Level I crossing guards do we have, and how many Level II?
So right now we're at-- Let's give you exact numbers...
If you don't have the numbers, could you just give us a ballpark?
Nope.
No, 2,219 Level I, and 90 are Level
So basically, all of them are Level I with very minor exceptions.

Right. So, typically, school crossing guards are maybe ten or more in a command, and then they have a Level II who is their supervisor and does the administrative side of the process, and there are one or two in a command.

Yup. And yet--and by the way, I really appreciate your point earlier. You were very clear, right? It seems like the pay structure makes it difficult for people to want to apply and also stay there. This is a very expensive city, $19.00 an hour, five hours a day, that's not

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 175 Committee on Public Safety going to get you anywhere. Won't be able to even purchase groceries with that. What is the process for requesting a school crossing guard, and how many requests do we receive per year?

So a typical request comes in either through school officials, parents, Level II, the CO themselves, the commanding officer of the Command, a borough coordinator, residents, or elected officials. It goes through the commanding officer to Command. He does an assessment, a risk-based assessment; he'll look at it. He'll look at pedestrian volume, he'll look at traffic volume, speed conditions, whether the location actually has a traffic signal or not, sight distance, and whether there are a lot of turns involved. Students age to students that actually go there, as well as, he'll look at collision data. Collision data is not the only thing they look at. There are many things. So, they'll make their assessment. It will go up through the borough and will come up to the Chief of Patrols' office. My office will take a look at it. We'll either concur. And then we'll send

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 176 Committee on Public Safety it over to Strategic Initiatives, who will do an assessment as well. Obviously, allocation comes into account as well. So there are a number of factors going into this. You'll see publicly displayed, as I said before, there are 2,639 school crossing guard posts posted publicly. Again, I'll tell you our headcount is at 2,219. So there is a gap there. A lot of those posts were historical. So basically, we know our headcount has to be evaluated, our actual count has to be evaluated, and these posts have to be evaluated, and they have to go into priority order. So we look at data and assessment to prioritize. You spoke about the location of the school that was mentioned to you, and the (INAUDIBLE) Precinct is very familiar with it, uh, 1910 Arthur Avenue. I spoke with the commanding officer, at that Command, we are doing an assessment at that location specifically. That command has 20 school crossing guards, and they're at their allocation of 20. So some schools require more than one school crossing guard, because the crossing is so

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 177 Committee on Public Safety dangerous. That's one way we like to keep our school crossing guard safe — double up posts. So we're always making these assessments, every year before the start of the year, we make that assessment, and we do our priority posts. Sometimes they move up, sometimes they move down. But our allocation is our allocation, our headcount is our headcount, and our post list is our post list. But there are a lot of decision makers, and we all come together and make that assessment.
All right. Thank you for that information. So the 2,219, is that the total headcount or is that the Level I headcount?
So that's the Level I, then you have another 90 on top of Level II guards, which will bring you to 2,309.
Got it. Okay.
So, Level II, just so you know, also fill in when there's a gap, or there's a vacancy, or there's a school crossing guard that may call out, so they'll assist as well.

Approximately--going back to the question, approximately how many

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 178 Committee on Public Safety applications do we-- or how many requests do we receive per year? And if there's no formal process, what would be a super rough number that you say, if you were to guess?
I don't want to guess. I don't have that number.
Would you say it's more than 1,000, 2,000, 3,000, 4,000, or 5,000? It’s a big city.

As a former commanding officer, two times, I frequently got requests for school crossing guards. Who wouldn't want a school crossing guard? Their beloved people, they are community members, they live in the command. They're out there day in and day out, in all types of weather. And they're just lovely people, so we get these requests quite often.
How’s retention in this division? How often do they usually, when hired, how long do they usually stay for?

So that's something I'd have to get back to as far as retention.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 179 Committee on Public Safety
Okay. If you don't have any data, is that an issue you've seen with the school crossing guards?

I painted a picture of our staffing. We're currently very close to our allocation. So we got the 100 who are in the class who are going to get hired on May 11th, and with the 45 long-term sick, we're at the allocation. So I think our recruitment efforts are working and are at the allocations.
